During the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya overpowers Sitaram by taking his weapon and tying him up from head to foot; however, on the night of Udayaditya's escape, Sitaram takes the lead by entering Udayaditya's prison cell and grabbing him to almost carry him out of the prison.

Pratapaditya's initial, failed plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray when he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore, and the method that finally succeeds in ending the old king's life is Abdul killing him with a drawn sword.

The Mahishi sent Matangini to secretly fetch medicine from Mangala, who prepared a poison through rituals and mantras so that the Yubaraj would feel no pity when Surma died.

As a result of Vibha's refusal, the King felt insulted and sought revenge by marrying another woman, which meant that when Vibha finally arrived, she found the King getting married, shattering her world and causing her hopes of happiness to vanish.

Udayaditya's ring, which had his name engraved on its seal, was used to stamp a forged petition that falsely claimed the Yubaraj was lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor. After Bhagavat delivered this petition to Pratapaditya, the Maharaj ordered Udayaditya to be imprisoned.

Ramchandra Ray's escape led to the dismissal of the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat. Udayaditya provided a monthly stipend to these dismissed guards, which enraged Pratapaditya and led him to decree that no one should provide them with any more financial help. When Surma secretly arranged to send stipends to Sitaram's mother and Bhagavat's wife, news of these secret payments reached Pratapaditya, prompting him to order that Surma be sent to her paternal home.

The emotional significance of the song is the sense of emptiness and loneliness caused by the absence of loved ones who are no longer there to answer his call or share in his joy. Basanta Ray sings it first while sitting on his veranda in Raigarh, gazing at the setting sun and thinking about how those he used to sing for are no longer present. He sings it a second time in Jessore, standing near the silent, dark, and empty room of Surma after being told that no one is in it.

Rukmini's failure to stop Udayaditya's midnight escape allowed him to reach Raigarh, where she later found him, leading to his capture and the delivery of the order for the death sentence of the King of Raigarh, Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya's initial reception of Ramchandra Ray was calm and indifferent; he treated Ramchandra like a boy and prioritized his own administrative business over the visit. In contrast, Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya's status in his own court by allowing and participating in daily verbal attacks and ridicule aimed at Pratapaditya's lineage and status.

She left Raigarh, changed her name to Mangala, and lives on the outskirts of Jessore. She befriends the palace servants to track news and uses her knowledge of tantra, mantra, and medicine to prepare a poison, disguised as medicine, which leads to Surma's death. She also re-enters Udayaditya's life by entering his bedchamber during a storm to confront him.

Udayaditya's early lament—wishing he had not been born the crown prince or sole heir because he felt unfit for the heavy burden of the kingdom—culminates when he is brought before his father, Pratapaditya, as a prisoner. He agrees with his father that he is unworthy of the kingdom and formally pleads for release from the throne. This culminates in a formal oath taken at the temple before Ma-Kali, where he swears he will never rule even a needle's tip of the land, will not sit on the throne of Jessore, and will not touch the royal scepter, opting instead to leave for Kashi to live as an ascetic.

Nayanchand intercepts the letter by taking it from Ramchandra Ray but, fearing Pratapaditya's reaction, gives it to the Mahishi instead of delivering it to Jessore. The letter is subsequently misrepresented when, after reading it and concluding it was written out of anger, Basanta Ray advises the Mahishi to announce to the household that Ramchandra Ray had actually written the letter to request that Vibha be sent to her in-laws' house.
Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the large Sal wood logs that had been used to block the canal.

Basanta Ray leaves his sitar behind when departing from Udayaditya, stating that he will no longer play it. Later, he explains that although he has the sitar, its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned, reflecting his sense of emptiness and his loss of joy after being left behind without his loved ones.

Udayaditya's former courage has gone, and he can no longer fight against oppression with all his might. While he previously would have stopped an official from beating a subject without considering the consequences, he now avoids intervening and instead runs into his house. Additionally, he no longer has the courage to help those in hardship with money, as he hesitates and fails to send it.
He tells Udayaditya that the prison is on fire and grabs him, almost carrying him out of the prison.

On the first occasion, Rammohan ties thick sheets together to make a rope, ties Ramchandra Ray to his back, climbs down the rope, and then grips the rope with his teeth to release Ramchandra into a boat before jumping down himself. On the second occasion, he lifts Vibha, brings her out of the palace, and places her into a palanquin.

In Jessore, Vibha is heavily adorned with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and a specific coiffure. When she seeks out Ramchandra Ray in Chandradwip, she dresses as a common woman or "beggar-woman" and refuses to use a palanquin.

In his bedchamber, the window is a place of longing where Udayaditya sits to occupy the empty spot where Surma used to sit, looking out at the garden and moonlight in the hope that she might appear. In the prison cell, the window symbolizes hope for freedom and liberation; watching the birds fly through it reminds him that his cage will one day break, and he considers the window a place where he is naturally free, whereas he views the bed as his prison.

Sitaram's relationship with Rukmini begins as a flirtatious arrangement where he uses witty banter and romantic names such as "Priyatame" and "Pranpriye" to borrow money from her. The dynamic shifts after Udayaditya's imprisonment, when Sitaram curses Rukmini and threatens to ruin her. The encounter becomes life-threatening when Sitaram enters Rukmini's cottage at night to steal her money, believing she is dead, only to find her in a terrifying, disheveled, and trembling state. When Sitaram attempts to use feigned affection to manage the situation, Rukmini reacts with intense rage, threatening to kill both him and the Yubaraj and searching for a curved blade, which forces Sitaram to flee.

Sitaram initiates the strategy by orchestrating a blaze in several rooms using loyal commoners and palace servants, while his men actively sabotage firefighting efforts to ensure the fire is not extinguished. He then has his men set fire to Udayaditya's empty prison cell, including its windows, doors, beams, and rafters. To complete the cover-up, Sitaram throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the burning room and then claims to the onlookers that the roof has collapsed and there is no response from the Yubaraj. This results in the rumor of Udayaditya's death, which is supported by witnesses who claim to have heard his screams and the discovery of his melted, burnt sword in the cell.

Ramchandra Ray was not grateful that Udayaditya had saved his life, believing it was bound to happen and that Udayaditya's main objective was actually saving his sister rather than saving Ramchandra himself. Consequently, in his court, he brought up Udayaditya's name to laugh and joke about him because he was Pratapaditya's son.

A forged petition is written and stamped with the Yubaraj's seal to make it appear as though the Yubaraj is lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor in order to obtain the kingdom for himself.

Vibha's hair serves as a marker because while Surma was present, Vibha would secretly go to her to have her hair done to her own liking; however, in Surma's absence, Vibha sits quietly waiting for Surma to braid it, but Surma never comes and Vibha's hair remains unbraided.
